item.title: Higher-Order Functions Are Not Free: The reduce That's Secretly O(n²)
item.description: There is a piece of advice that gets repeated until it sounds like a law: prefer map, filter, and reduce over a for loop, because they are more efficient. The first half is reasonable. The second half is wrong, and believing it has cost us real frame time. Higher-order functions are a readability tool, not a speed tool, and at least one of them has a default that turns an innocent one-liner into O(n²).

item.title: How Closures Capture, and Why Your Screen Leaks
item.description:
Closures get introduced as “functions you can pass around,” which is true and also the least interesting thing about them. The part that decides whether your app leaks memory is capture: a closure quietly grabs the things it references and keeps them alive. Get that wrong with the wrong closure and you have the single most common memory bug in iOS, a view controller that never deallocates.

So let’s skip the map { $0 * 2 } tour and talk about what a closure actually holds onto.

item.title: The Hidden Cost of Value Types: Copy-on-Write, and When Structs Bite
item.description:
“Use structs by default” is advice so repeated that nobody asks the obvious follow-up: what does the copy actually cost? Everyone can recite that structs copy and classes share. The part worth your attention is what “copy” means at runtime, when it is free, when it quietly is not, and the class of bug that shows up when you have lost track of which one you are holding.

We will assume you know the textbook difference. Assign a struct, you get an independent copy. Assign a class, both names point at the same instance. Here is everything past that.

item.title: What Swift's Optional Really Is, and When to Stop Reaching for It
item.description: Optionals get taught once, as “the box that might be empty,” and then everyone moves on to unwrapping syntax and never looks back. That is a shame, because the interesting part is not how to open the box. It is what Optional actually is, the two or three places it behaves in ways that surprise people years in, and the design question nobody frames: when is an optional the right tool, and when is it just you not modeling the problem?

item.title: Modeling the Current User Without a Global Singleton
item.description:
Almost every app has the line. User.current, or Session.shared, or AppState.user. A global you can reach from anywhere that holds the logged-in user. It is the most convenient object in the codebase on day one and, a year later, the most coupled. The profile module is usually where the rot shows up first, because profile screens read and write the current user more than anywhere else.

So let’s not design “a UserProfile module.” Let’s design the thing that actually decides whether your app stays testable: how the current user is modeled and reached.

item.title: Data Flow From API to UI: The Parts That Actually Break
item.description:
Drawing the layers for API-to-UI data flow is the part everyone can do: networking fetches, a view model holds state, the view renders. Boxes and arrows, done in an interview in two minutes. That diagram is also where the real problems are not. The hard parts of data flow are the ones the diagram hides, and they are where shipping apps actually break.

Here is a snippet close to what a lot of view models really contain. It looks reasonable. It has a bug that ships to production constantly.

item.title: Why UIKit Pushes You Into a Massive View Controller
item.description:
Every iOS team eventually fights the same file. A view controller that started small and is now four figures of line count, the one nobody volunteers to touch. The usual explanation is discipline: someone got lazy, nobody refactored. That explanation is comfortable and mostly wrong.

Massive View Controller is not a discipline failure. It is what UIKit’s design pushes you toward by default. If you understand the mechanism, you stop fighting symptoms and start removing the actual causes. So let’s look at why the controller becomes a magnet, and then at what each escape hatch genuinely costs, because none of them are free.

item.title: Everything about Error Handling in Combine
item.description:
Everything about Error Handling in Combine

In the previous article, while discussing the 5 essential caveats to remember to master Combine, we touched upon error handling briefly. In this article, we will dive deep into error handling in Combine, covering everything there is about built in error handling in Combine.

This article is part of a series where I dive deep into iOS concepts, exploring the smallest details often overlooked by typical articles. I aim to blend definitions with practical insights for a clear and actionable understanding. Whether you’re a seasoned developer or eager to learn, this series will provide the insights and skills needed to master these powerful frameworks. Let’s get started.

item.title: Mastering Swift Combine: 5 Essential Caveats to Remember
item.description:
Mastering Swift Combine: 5 Essential Caveats to Remember

Combine framework’s caveats: Learn key pitfalls and actionable insights for effective integration into your code.

Combine, Apple’s own reactive programming framework, holds immense potential. However, effectively using its capabilities demands one to be aware of specific caveats and pitfalls.

This article explores these caveats and provides actionable insights for integrating Combine effectively into your code. While some considerations here may seem intuitive, they are often overlooked until you grasp Combine thoroughly.
